question_text: How would you design a URL shortener like bit.ly? Walk through your approach.
correct_answer: Generate a short code (6-7 chars base62) mapped to the original URL stored in a database. Use a counter or random generation with collision checking. Store in Redis for fast lookups with DB as persistent store. On short URL access, lookup in Redis first (cache-aside), then DB, then redirect 301/302. Scale with read replicas for the lookup-heavy workload. Rate limit creation. Use CDN to cache redirects. Handle custom aliases, expiry, and analytics.
key_points: Short code: base62 encoding of counter or hash
Redis cache for O(1) redirects
301 (permanent) vs 302 (temporary) redirect implications for analytics
Scale read path with caching — writes are rare vs reads
tip: Discuss 301 vs 302 tradeoff: 301 browsers cache so you lose analytics; 302 hits your server every time.

question_text: Design a notification system for a platform with 10 million users.
correct_answer: Use a message queue (Kafka, SQS) to decouple notification generation from delivery. Fan-out service reads events and creates per-user notification tasks. Worker pool processes tasks and calls appropriate delivery channels: push (FCM/APNs), email (SES/SendGrid), SMS (Twilio). Store notification history in Cassandra or DynamoDB for high write throughput. Retry failed deliveries with exponential backoff. User preference table controls which channels they want.
key_points: Message queue decouples event generation from delivery
Fan-out pattern for multi-channel delivery
Cassandra/DynamoDB for high-write notification storage
Retry with exponential backoff for failed deliveries
tip: Distinguish push notifications needing user devices registration (FCM/APNs) from email/SMS.

question_text: What is CAP theorem and how does it affect your database choice?
correct_answer: CAP theorem states a distributed system can only guarantee two of three: Consistency (all nodes see same data), Availability (every request gets a response), Partition tolerance (works during network splits). Since network partitions always happen, you choose CP (consistent, may be unavailable) or AP (available, may be stale). PostgreSQL/MySQL are CP. DynamoDB and Cassandra are AP (eventual consistency). Choose based on whether stale reads or unavailability is worse for your use case.
key_points: Partition tolerance is mandatory — choose C or A
CP: PostgreSQL, MySQL — consistent but may reject requests
AP: Cassandra, DynamoDB — always available, eventually consistent
Banking/payments need CP; social feeds can tolerate AP
tip: Give a concrete example: banking balance must be consistent (CP); Instagram likes can be eventual (AP).

question_text: How would you design a rate limiter for an API that handles 1 million requests per second?
correct_answer: Use Redis with sliding window or token bucket algorithm. Token bucket: each user has N tokens refilled at rate R per second. Decrement on each request, reject when empty. Use Redis MULTI/EXEC for atomic operations or Lua scripts. For distributed rate limiting, use Redis cluster. For 1M RPS, shard by user ID across Redis nodes. Edge rate limiting at CDN (Cloudflare) reduces origin load. Return 429 with Retry-After header.
key_points: Token bucket or sliding window counter algorithms
Redis atomic operations via Lua script or pipeline
Shard Redis by user ID for horizontal scaling
Edge/CDN rate limiting handles burst before reaching API
tip: Lua script in Redis ensures atomicity: check + decrement happens as one operation.

question_text: Explain the differences between SQL and NoSQL databases. When do you choose each?
correct_answer: SQL databases are relational with fixed schemas, ACID transactions, and powerful join queries — ideal for structured data with complex relationships. NoSQL covers document (MongoDB), key-value (Redis), columnar (Cassandra), and graph (Neo4j) — each optimized for specific access patterns. Choose SQL for: financial data, complex queries, data integrity. Choose NoSQL for: high write throughput, flexible schema, horizontal scaling, or specific access patterns like time-series or graphs.
key_points: SQL: ACID, joins, fixed schema, vertical scaling
NoSQL: flexible schema, horizontal scaling, high throughput
Choose based on access patterns not just scale
Polyglot persistence: use both in the same system
tip: Mention polyglot persistence — Postgres for user data, Redis for sessions, S3 for files, Elasticsearch for search.

question_text: How would you design a real-time chat system for 1 million concurrent users?
correct_answer: WebSockets for persistent connections. Use a connection pool manager to route users to the right server. Message broker (Kafka or Redis Pub/Sub) broadcasts messages across servers — when user A on server 1 sends to user B on server 2, message goes through broker. Store messages in Cassandra (high write throughput, time-series optimal). Presence service tracks online status. Load balancer with sticky sessions or consistent hashing routes reconnections.
key_points: WebSockets for bidirectional persistent connections
Redis Pub/Sub or Kafka for cross-server message fan-out
Cassandra for message storage (time-series, high writes)
Presence service tracks online/offline status at scale
tip: Explain fan-out: user in group chat with 1000 members — fan-out sends to 1000 WebSocket connections.

question_text: What is consistent hashing and why is it used in distributed systems?
correct_answer: Consistent hashing maps both data and servers onto a ring. Data is assigned to the nearest server clockwise on the ring. When a server is added or removed, only the data on the adjacent section moves — O(K/N) keys move vs O(K) in naive modular hashing. This minimizes cache invalidation and data movement during scaling events. Used in CDNs, distributed caches (Memcached), and database sharding.
key_points: Data and nodes mapped to same hash ring
Only adjacent data moves when node added/removed
Virtual nodes improve distribution uniformity
Used in CDN, Memcached, Cassandra, DynamoDB
tip: Virtual nodes (vnodes): each physical server gets 100-200 positions on ring for better load distribution.

question_text: How do you design a search feature for an e-commerce platform?
correct_answer: Elasticsearch is the industry standard for full-text search. Index product data from the primary database using CDC (Change Data Capture) to sync changes. Implement inverted index for keyword search. Use analyzers for stemming and tokenization. Implement faceted search for filters (brand, price range, category). Relevance scoring with BM25 + business boosts (inventory, margins). Autocomplete via prefix queries or specialized suggest API. Redis caches popular searches.
key_points: Elasticsearch for full-text search with inverted index
CDC sync (Debezium) keeps search index fresh from DB
Faceted filters via Elasticsearch aggregations
Redis caches top 1000 search queries for instant results
tip: Explain the database + search index dual write problem and why CDC is better than dual write.

question_text: What is a CDN and how does it improve application performance?
correct_answer: A CDN (Content Delivery Network) is a geographically distributed network of servers that caches static assets close to users. When a user requests content, it routes to the nearest CDN edge server (PoP) rather than the origin, reducing latency from hundreds of ms to single-digit ms. Caches: images, JS, CSS, videos, and API responses with appropriate TTL. CDNs also provide DDoS protection, SSL termination, and serve as the first line of request routing.
key_points: Edge servers cache content geographically near users
Cache-Control headers control TTL at CDN
Reduces latency, origin load, and bandwidth costs
Cloudflare, AWS CloudFront, Fastly are popular CDNs
tip: Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000 for versioned assets; no-cache for HTML.

question_text: Explain the difference between horizontal and vertical scaling.
correct_answer: Vertical scaling (scale up) adds more CPU/RAM to a single machine — simple but has physical limits and single point of failure. Horizontal scaling (scale out) adds more machines — infinitely scalable, highly available, but requires stateless design and load balancing. Stateless services (no server-stored sessions) scale horizontally easily. Databases need sharding or read replicas for horizontal scaling. Most modern systems use a combination.
key_points: Vertical: more resources on one machine, simple, limited
Horizontal: more machines, requires stateless architecture
Load balancer distributes traffic across horizontal fleet
Database scaling: read replicas for reads, sharding for writes
tip: Session management challenge: horizontal scaling requires Redis session store or JWT (stateless tokens).

question_text: How would you design the data model for a social media feed (like Twitter)?
correct_answer: Two approaches: fan-out on write (push) stores the feed pre-computed per user — fast reads, expensive writes for users with many followers. Fan-out on read (pull) assembles feed at query time — expensive reads for users following many accounts. Hybrid: pre-compute for regular users, compute on read for celebrity accounts with millions of followers. Store posts in Cassandra time-partitioned by (user_id, month). Use Redis for hot feed caching.
key_points: Fan-out on write: pre-computed feeds, fast reads
Fan-out on read: assembled at query time, expensive for large follows
Hybrid: push for normal users, pull for celebrities
Cassandra for posts: time-series, high write throughput
tip: The celebrity problem: Elon Musk has 100M followers — fan-out on write = 100M writes per tweet.

question_text: What is database indexing and what are the tradeoffs?
correct_answer: Indexes speed up read queries by creating a secondary data structure (typically B-tree) that the database scans instead of the full table. A query filtering by an indexed column goes from O(n) full scan to O(log n) index lookup. Tradeoffs: indexes consume disk space, and every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must update all indexes — slowing writes. Over-indexing hurts write-heavy workloads. Composite indexes must match query column order. EXPLAIN ANALYZE reveals if indexes are used.
key_points: B-tree index: O(log n) lookup vs O(n) full scan
Every write must update all indexes — write overhead
Composite index order matters for partial use
EXPLAIN ANALYZE to verify index usage in queries
tip: Show how EXPLAIN ANALYZE changes from Seq Scan to Index Scan — proves real performance impact.

question_text: How do microservices communicate with each other — synchronous vs asynchronous?
correct_answer: Synchronous: REST HTTP or gRPC — caller waits for response. Simple but creates tight coupling; if downstream service is slow, caller is slow. Asynchronous: message queue (Kafka, RabbitMQ) — caller publishes event and continues. Consumer processes at its own pace. Async improves resilience and decouples services but adds eventual consistency. Use sync for operations needing immediate response (auth check, payment status). Use async for notifications, email, analytics, and workflows.
key_points: Sync: REST/gRPC — immediate response, tight coupling
Async: Kafka/RabbitMQ — decoupled, eventual consistency
Sync for: user-facing real-time responses
Async for: notifications, analytics, background jobs
tip: Saga pattern for distributed transactions across microservices — choreography vs orchestration.

question_text: What is the Saga pattern and how does it manage distributed transactions?
correct_answer: A Saga is a sequence of local transactions where each step publishes an event triggering the next step. If any step fails, compensating transactions undo previous steps. Two implementations: choreography (services react to events, no central coordinator — simpler but hard to trace) and orchestration (central orchestrator directs services — easier to visualize but single point of failure). Used when ACID transactions across microservices are impossible.
key_points: Sequence of local transactions with compensating rollbacks
Choreography: event-driven, decentralized, harder to trace
Orchestration: central coordinator, easier to visualize
Replaces ACID transactions in distributed systems
tip: Order service Saga: reserve stock → charge payment → confirm order. Failure at payment → release stock.

question_text: How would you approach designing a system for 10x traffic growth?
correct_answer: Start by identifying the bottleneck: load test to find the breaking point. Usually the database breaks first. Solutions: add read replicas, implement caching (Redis), add CDN for static assets, queue background jobs to offload the API, and scale horizontally with load balancer. Profile before optimizing — N+1 queries, missing indexes, and missing caches often 10x performance before infrastructure changes. Plan for stateless services from the start.
key_points: Load test first — find actual bottleneck
Database usually breaks first — add read replicas + cache
CDN removes static asset load from origin servers
Stateless services enable horizontal scaling
tip: The 80/20 rule: most performance gains come from caching and query optimization, not hardware.
